summary: This RFC updates RFC 3315 so a DHCPv6 Reconfigure message may ask the client to send a Rebind message. It also clarifies how a client responds to a Reconfigure message it receives.

eli5.summary: A server can tap a client and say go ask all the servers again. This adds one more thing it may ask the client to do.

questions: can dhcpv6 reconfigure trigger a rebind
how does a dhcpv6 client respond to reconfigure
what is msg-type 6 in dhcpv6 reconfigure
subtitle: Lets a DHCPv6 server tell a client to send a Rebind, so the client can be moved to a different server.

tldr.problem: In DHCPv6 a Reconfigure message could only make a client send Renew or Information-request, and Renew goes to one named server. That does not help when a server is shut down and its clients must talk to a different one.
tldr.mechanism: The Reconfigure Message option may now carry msg-type 6 (Rebind). A Rebind has no Server Identifier option, so any server can answer. The RFC also pins down which server a Renew should name.
tldr.outcome: A server can push clients toward other servers on demand. Because that is also an attack opportunity, clients that support it MUST implement Reconfigure Key authentication.

today: RFC 6644 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3315, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Reconfigure Needs Rebind
sections.content:
In DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) a server may send an unsolicited Reconfigure message to a client. The client answers with a Renew or an Information-request, depending on the msg-type field in the Reconfigure Message option. A Renew includes a Server Identifier option naming the server that should respond, so this only works when the client keeps talking to the same servers.

The RFC gives a scenario where that fails: an administrator shuts down a DHCPv6 server and wants the clients that most recently used it to move to a different server. Allowing the server to ask for a Rebind, which carries no Server Identifier option, lets any server respond.

The RFC also fills a gap. RFC 3315 did not say the Reconfigure must come from the server the client last talked to, nor which server a Renew should identify. This document clarifies the second point.
sections.eli5: If your usual helper is leaving, you cannot keep asking only that helper. The new rule lets the helper say: ask anyone who is here.

sections.title: The Reconfigure Message Option
sections.content:
The change to the option is small. Its format is OPTION_RECONF_MSG (option code 19) followed by an option-len of 1 and a one-octet msg-type. The RFC lists three values: 5 for Renew, 6 for Rebind and 11 for Information-request.

The server uses this option to select which of the three messages the client responds with. Value 6 is the addition made by this document, which modifies Section 22.19 of RFC 3315.
sections.eli5: The note the server sends has one small box that says which of three things to do. This RFC adds a third choice to that box.

sections.title: What Servers Do
sections.content:
The RFC rewrites parts of Sections 19.1 and 19.2 of RFC 3315 in OLD and NEW form. The server MUST include a Reconfigure Message option selecting Renew, Rebind or Information-request, and MUST NOT include other options except as specifically allowed. It sends each Reconfigure to a single client by unicast, directly or through a relay agent using a Relay-reply message. To reconfigure many clients it unicasts a separate message to each.

The server counts a received Renew, Rebind or Information-request, whichever was requested, as satisfying the Reconfigure. If none arrives in REC_TIMEOUT milliseconds, it retransmits, doubles the timeout and waits again. After REC_MAX_RC unsuccessful attempts it SHOULD abort for that client.

Section 19.2 now covers Renew and Rebind separately. A Renew gets a Reply as described in Sections 18.2.3 and 18.2.8, and a Rebind gets a Reply as described in Sections 18.2.4 and 18.2.8. The Reply MAY include IAs and other parameters even if the client did not request them.
sections.eli5: The server taps each client one by one. If a client does not answer, the server taps again, waiting longer each time, and finally gives up.

sections.title: What Clients Do
sections.content:
On a valid Reconfigure the client now responds with a Renew, a Rebind or an Information-request, as the option indicates. It ignores the transaction-id of the Reconfigure, and silently discards other Reconfigure messages while its transaction is in progress.

New text for Section 19.4.2 says the client builds the Rebind exactly as in Section 18.1.4 of RFC 3315, except that it copies the Option Request option and any IA options from the Reconfigure into the Rebind. If a client is already sending Rebind messages, it ignores any received Reconfigure.

Section 19.4.4 is updated so the same variables and retransmission algorithm apply as for client-initiated Renew, Rebind or Information-request. If no response arrives by the end of retransmission, the client ignores and discards the Reconfigure.
sections.eli5: When the client gets the tap, it asks the way it was told to. It copies the questions from the tap into its own request. If it is already asking everyone, it ignores new taps.

sections.title: Clarification for Renew
sections.content:
Section 6 clarifies Section 19.4.2 of RFC 3315. When a client sends a Renew in response to a Reconfigure, it MUST include a Server Identifier option identifying the server with which it most recently communicated.

The introduction describes the intent: the client names the same server it would have named had it sent the Renew after timer T1 expired.
sections.eli5: If the client is told to ask its usual helper again, it must say that helper's name, the same one it would have used anyway.

sections.title: Spoofed Reconfigure Risk
sections.content:
Allowing Rebind in a Reconfigure creates an attack. An attacker could send a faked Reconfigure to push a client off its current server, then answer the client's Rebind quickly and link it to a fake server. The RFC notes that a similar attack already exists when an attacker poses as a valid DHCPv6 server in answer to a Solicit or Request.

These attacks can be prevented with the AUTH option. DHCPv6 clients that support Reconfigure-Rebind MUST implement the Reconfigure Key authentication protocol from Section 21.5 of RFC 3315. Other mechanisms may be added; the RFC mentions Secure DHCPv6 based on Cryptographically Generated Addresses as one example, then still a work in progress.
sections.eli5: A stranger could pretend to be the server and send the client to a fake helper. So the client must check a secret password the real server shares before it obeys the tap.

items.label: Renew
items.desc: Client sends Renew, naming the server in a Server Identifier option.

items.label: Rebind
items.desc: Added by this RFC. Client sends Rebind with no Server Identifier, so any server may answer.
